The systematic review on indoor heat for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines assesses the health effects of indoor temperatures above 24°C. The review aims to provide evidence to inform the deliberations of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The report includes background information, eligibility criteria, search strategies, data extraction methods, findings, and discussions. It also contains comprehensive appendices with detailed information. Heat is a natural hazard that can impair the human body's thermoregulation, leading to adverse health effects. Epidemiological studies have primarily focused on outdoor ambient temperature as the exposure, concluding that increased outdoor temperatures independently affect mortality. However, most people, especially those over 65, spend the majority of their time indoors during summer, suggesting that indoor heat exposure may pose significant health risks. Building energy codes and standards aim to maintain indoor environments within reasonable thermal bounds. While some standards focus on thermal comfort, defined as the condition of mind expressing satisfaction with the thermal environment, they do not explicitly address health aspects. This review seeks to establish a link between indoor temperatures and health to inform upper indoor temperature thresholds. The eligibility criteria for the review include studies examining the health effects of indoor temperatures above 24°C. The threshold of 24°C is not definitive but serves as a reference point for identifying relevant literature. The review also considers the duration of heat exposure and its health effects, as well as the role of factors like humidity and ventilation. Vulnerable populations, such as older adults, infants, and individuals with illnesses, are given special attention. Search strategies involved indexed bibliographic databases, including Embase, Greenfile, MEDLINE, and others, with searches conducted in January 2015. Records were restricted to those published from 2004 onwards. A total of 10,200 records were retrieved, and 137 full-text articles were identified as potentially relevant. Two reviewers independently assessed the records for relevance, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The review focused on English-language abstracts, assuming that pivotal research would be accessible in English. The systematic review highlights the importance of understanding the health risks associated with indoor heat exposure and aims to provide evidence to guide policy and interventions.
